blocks.heading: 6.3 Buffers are a priced decision
blocks.markdown: Buffers need not sit idle. Borg reports about 20% of a median cell's workload running in reclaimed resources [17]. A backfill policy must say whether batch tenants pay for the buffer they borrow.

blocks.heading: 6.4 Bridges and clearing
blocks.markdown:
Picture the 9 p.m. shortage email: approved ask, late machines, launch still on the calendar. When approved demand can't be sourced in time, you bridge. The levers differ in speed and premium (speeds are my judgment of orders of magnitude, not sourced figures):

| Bridge | Time to capacity | Main cost |
|---|---|---|
| Reclaim idle or over-held capacity | Days to weeks | Effort; friction with the holder |
| Shift demand across regions or time | Hours to weeks for stateless serving; longer for stateful | Latency, data residency, migration |
| Reallocate between tenants | Weeks | Migration; churn |
| Re-peg supply from a slipped launch to an on-time one | Days | Effort; the slipped launch re-confirms its date |
| Defer decommission of older hardware | Weeks, if not yet retired and if its space and power aren't needed by incoming hardware | Power, efficiency and reliability penalty |
| Third-party capacity | Months, with a standing agreement; longer without one | Price premium; capital becomes operating spend; usually a minimum term of its own |
| Facility redesign or retrofit | Quarters to years | Capital |

Shifting demand is routine at scale: Flux reports global workload shifts every six weeks, each "reshuffling capacity for 100k-300k servers globally" [2]. In the SRE chapter's Meet case, capacity came partly from "borrowing machine resources from other teams across Google," a tenant-to-tenant bridge run under incident pressure [7]. Oversubscription is left out on purpose: it's better run as a standing policy, backed by peak prediction and power capping, than as an emergency lever [85–87]. The SRE chapter's pooled quota runs it that way [7]. Microsoft reports that predicting power peaks enabled "a 2× increase in oversubscription with minimum impact to critical workloads" [A3]. A later Borg study reports production compute usage at "only around 30% of the allocated level," with over-commitment as a standing bet [88].

**A bridge has a lead time too.** It works on your clock only if it was arranged before you needed it, so a standing third-party agreement is itself a slow-layer option. Power can be bridged too, with temporary on-site generation [60] (Appendix B).

**Pegging makes the cheapest bridge possible.** Supply planners link every order to the demand it was placed for; they call it *pegging*. It lets a late delivery be traced to the launches it hits, and a slipped launch to the deliveries it can hand to someone else. In my experience launches and deliveries both tend to run late, so the two can often cancel out, but only if the link exists.

**Every bridge carries a premium, and the premium has a cause:** a late ask, a forecast miss, an off-cycle launch. Treat it as a cost driver and send it there; spread across everyone, it teaches that late asks are free. When the cause is a shared service that recovers its costs through its rate, hold the premium outside that rate, or it reaches every caller.

**Clearing** is the other half: one team holds capacity it doesn't need, another needs exactly that shape, there, now. Matching them is what Jevons called a "double coincidence" [89]: the baker who wants shoes must find a shoemaker who wants bread. Done by people **brokering** trades, it's a market with no price, and it scales poorly; the quota auctions and markets of Section 3 try to give it one [16, 18]. RAS automates part of it within one operator's region-wide server reservations [54]. The Quota Marketplace preprint does so for ML training accelerators, with teams bidding credits from an income that administrators "assign … to reflect their relative priority" [18]. The authors report average occupancy of 93% against 75% in a comparable conventional pool. That's the operator's observational comparison, not a controlled experiment, and occupancy is not goodput (useful progress; Section 11). Because the market can't see which accelerators share an interconnect domain, it produces preemptions "where quota exists but geometry does not" in about 1% of cases.

So markets automate clearing for fungible, short-horizon resources, and human work moves to weights, envelopes, shapes and long-lead supply, where the calendar, not just the shape, decides the outcome.

Human clearing runs on information. For example, if one team has spare cores but needs memory in three regions this quarter, someone has to find the other half. The trade clears only if someone already knows which team holds that memory there and needs the cores. Four things must match at once: the resource, the amount, the place and the time. That knowledge comes from a weekly habit of asking teams what's coming and what's idle, more than from any report. That's also why Section 10.4 says to log every trade: what the broker knows should outlive the broker.

blocks.heading: 6.5 Two clocks
blocks.markdown:
*In short: the slower a supply layer, the earlier you must order it and the less you know when you do. For persistent demand in a growing portfolio, this paper argues for aiming higher in the range.*

Go back to the launch of Section 5.4: a rumor, then a date, then a configuration. The power for its building may have been ordered before anyone heard the rumor. Demand information and supply commitments run on different clocks. Alphabet's chief executive put the supply side in one line: "how we close the gap this year is a function of what we have done in the prior years" [90].

Each supply layer is committed at its own commit point: its need date minus its cautious lead time (Section 6.2). Hixson and Guliani advise planning at least as far ahead as the order time, and answer unresolved demand with fungibility [6]; this section works that out layer by layer. What matters for each layer is the **residual uncertainty at its commit point**. That's how much of the declaration is still open when the layer must be ordered, and how sure its arrival date is. Hixson and Guliani point at a closely related quantity. They tell finance to check "the sensitivity that those estimates have to their time horizon and how far into the future people are being asked to forecast" [6].

Figure 22 draws the two clocks as lanes. On top, the declaration's open range narrows at decision events (diamonds). Below, each supply layer's bar is its lead time, its dot the commit point, and the orange bracket above the dot the residual then. Land, power and shell commits before any declaration exists, with the whole range open. For simplicity every bar ends at launch; since each layer must be ready before the next starts, slow layers really commit earlier than drawn (Section 8 does it properly).

Put Section 7's launch on it. Machines and parts commit at −6 months, when the declaration is Dated: a base of 60,000 and a high of 90,000 requests per second. That leaves a 30,000 spread still open, and, as Section 7 shows, the launch could still land below the base. Network commits at −15, at Intent: 40,000 to 100,000, so 60,000 open. The further left the dot, the wider the bracket. The table generalizes Figure 22 and adds physical placement (commit points are illustrative and vary by operator and market):

blocks.heading: 6.5 Two clocks
blocks.markdown:
| Supply layer | Typical commit point | Where the declaration usually is by then | Instrument |
|---|---|---|---|
| Land, power, building shell | One to several years ahead | Intent, or none | An envelope sized for the portfolio, not one launch; options; a fungible specification (Section 6.2) |
| Long-haul network; large supply contracts | Several quarters | Intent to dated | Buy toward the high, as options or with cancel windows |
| Machines and parts | One to three quarters | Dated | Buy to the base; hold the high as options, a launch reserve or a named bridge |
| Physical placement (site, hall, power domain) | With the machine order, or at turn-up | Dated to configured | A placement plan; spread across failure domains |
| Turn-up and allocation | Weeks per job; the rate is staffed months ahead | Configured | Rank against supply; move the cut line (the line on the ranked list below which asks go unfunded); issue grants; book turn-up slots |
| Job placement and admission | Minutes to days | Live | Bridges (shift, reclaim, defer decommission); admission control as the last line |

**Buy slow layers toward the high scenario.** A shortage lasts as long as the short layer takes to fix or bridge: weeks for turn-up, quarters for machines, years for power when no third-party space is available. An excess costs the layer's carrying cost (Section 6.3) until growth absorbs it, which depends on the growth rate, not the lead time. And per unit of compute it enables, a slow layer is cheap to carry. Where power is paid for as drawn, an empty powered hall costs far less than a shortage of the machines it would hold. Take-or-pay power or a leased shell narrows that gap. So the cost of being short rises with lead time while, for shells and power, the cost of being over doesn't rise much. In this paper's argument (not a published result), the shortage-to-idle ratio therefore rises with lead time. Illustratively, for persistent demand in a growing portfolio:

| Layer | Shortage : idle cost | Fraction | Buy to about |
|---|---|---|---|
| Turn-up | 1 : 1 | 1/(1 + 1) = 0.50 | The median |
| Machines | 4 : 1 | 4/(4 + 1) = 0.80 | The 80th percentile |
| Power and shell | 19 : 1 | 19/(19 + 1) = 0.95 | The 95th percentile |

Turn-up is the exception: it's a rate you staff (Section 6.2), so its ratio sets how much rate to staff, not how much to buy. Figure 23 draws the table as three ranges.

figure.caption: Figure 23. For lasting demand in a growing business, the paper argues that the cover point should rise with lead time: median for turn-up, about the 80th percentile for machines, about the 95th for power and shells. Illustrative, not a published result.

Notes give the two conditions: layers must work together, and the high is held mostly as options. Illustrative; the paper's argument, not a published result.

blocks.heading: 6.5 Two clocks
blocks.markdown:
Two conditions keep that sound:

1. **The layers have to work together** (economists call them complements). A high quantile on power pays only if machines can still be bought once demand firms; that postponement lets the fast layers stay at the base. The "warm shells" remark of Section 6.2 is this condition failing the other way.
2. **"High" is a big amount at the slow end,** where the open range is widest. Hold it mostly as options (Section 6.2).

One operator publishes the slow end of this: it plans "to a high quantile demand forecast" because "the cost of empty data center space is much less than the shortage cost of not being able to deploy compute and storage when needed" [8]. Its per-component quantiles, chosen to meet on-time delivery targets [8], show the quantile already varying by resource. Meta's chief executive put the argument in operator terms: "aggressively front-load building capacity so that way we're prepared for the most optimistic cases"; if superintelligence takes longer to arrive, "we'll use the extra compute to accelerate our core business," and in the worst case "slow building new infrastructure for some period while we grow into what we build" [74]. That last clause is the carrying cost of excess, paid as a pause in building. Meta's finance chief said in July 2026: "we believe near term capacity is more valuable than long term capacity" [91].

The argument weakens if growth stalls, since excess then waits years, not quarters. It also weakens if leased or third-party space can bridge the slow layer, or if the launches behind the high scenario share a driver (Section 6.6). For a transient step, or a launch that may not happen, the cost of being over is the whole unit. There, the high belongs in options and bridges, not owned capacity.

**Specify in lead-time order.** The clocks can move toward each other: in Figure 22, supply can slide its dots right, and demand can narrow its range sooner. Supply does it with shorter lead times, which Hixson and Guliani count among the most valuable things a company can do to cut planning risk and cost [6]. The SRE chapter says the same: faster supply shrinks "the window of time for which you actually need to predict capacity" [7]. It also does it with contracts that allow cancelling or pushing a delivery out. Demand does it most cheaply through what the intake asks first. Size and date usually firm last. But what drives the slowest supply (region, redundancy tier, hardware class and power density, data stored) is, in my experience, often decided early and not asked. The chapter describes the supply-side twin: bringing spatial awareness of datacenter footprints into "the long-range planning process" early, so demand forecasts are physically achievable [7]. Ask for it at the dated stage, with size as a range. For the slowest layer even that is too late; only the portfolio envelope can serve it.

**Place the gates between the events.** A planning gate is most useful just after the demand event that resolves something and just before the supply commit point that needs it. In Figure 22, that's between a diamond and the next dot. When a commit point falls before its event, as Appendix A's high-memory order does, there are three choices:

1. Ask for the decision earlier.
2. Buy an option that carries the commitment past the event.
3. Commit to the stage's record and name the owner of the residual.

Write down which you chose: what was known, when, by whom, and what would have changed it. Figure 24 walks the choice for one layer, with Appendix A's case.

**Bound how much the declaration may still move.** Buying against the range open at a commit point works only if the declaration then stays inside it. Manufacturing's *time fences* handle this (the closer an order is to its date, the less it may change), as do quantity-flexibility contracts (Section 6.2). One way to apply it here is a *change band* per stage. For example, say an intent may move by half in either direction, a dated ask by a quarter and a configured ask by a tenth. Then a change inside the band is the plan working. One outside it becomes a priced event recorded against the declaration, not a surprise (Section 8, step 7). Figure 25 shows where the gates go and how the bands narrow.

blocks.heading: 6.6 Timing, size and persistence
blocks.markdown:
*In short: a launch can be wrong on size or on timing, can last days or years, and can share a driver with other launches. Each changes what to buy and who pays.*

A size miss is paid for on what was bought for the size, mostly the slow and middle layers. Too high, and capacity waits for later demand; too low, and the gap needs bridges. A timing miss is, in my experience, most often a slip. It's paid for on everything committed for the launch, for the length of the slip, but shows mostly at the machine and turn-up layers. For example, if a building serves twenty launches, one arriving six weeks late hardly registers; the machines turned up for it do.

Section 5.2's variance decomposition shows neither error as what it is. A size miss shows as a smaller bill; a slip may not show at all, depending on how the consumer is billed:

| | Billed on realized peak, held flat for the year (Section 7's rule) | Billed on coincident-peak contribution, hour by hour |
|---|---|---|
| **Size miss** | A smaller bill (volume term) | A smaller bill (volume term) |
| **Slip** | Invisible: the consumer pays for the slipped weeks as if it had launched on time | The bill drops for those weeks; their cost moves to the service's unused line |

Capacity bought for demand that never arrives is billed to no one under either rule; it lands on the unused line. The service owner owns that line (mechanism 4), but the cost isn't booked to the declaration that caused it unless grants expire (Section 9.3). Each error needs its own owner.

**Persistence is the second distinction.** A *transient* step (a sale, a live broadcast, a launch-day spike) needs capacity for days; a *persistent* step (a new product, a new region), for years. Transient demand wants capacity that can be returned: shifted work, reclaimed and borrowed buffers, and third-party capacity. At the top of the peak, it wants admission control, the limit Alibaba accepts for an event it can predict but not plan for [33]. Persistent demand wants owned capacity. Many launches are both, a spike on a step. Size owned capacity on the spike and you buy permanent capacity for a temporary peak, so a declaration should carry the two shapes separately. Figure 26 shows what each kind of miss costs, and the two shapes.

figure.caption: Figure 26. A size miss is paid on the slow and middle layers; a slip, on the machines and turn-up committed for the launch. A spike on a step needs two shapes: owned capacity for the step, returnable capacity for the spike. On a flat bill, a slip can be invisible. Schematic.
figure.alt: Four panels. (a) A size miss is paid mostly on the slow and middle layers: too high, and capacity waits for demand; too low, and the gap needs bridges. (b) A slip is paid mostly at the machine and turn-up layers, for the length of the slip. A building serving twenty launches hardly notices one six weeks late. blocks.heading: 6.6 Timing, size and persistence
blocks.markdown:
**The third distinction is correlation.** Hixson and Guliani suggest planning for only some of several launches to succeed, "a very specific way to trade increased risk for the organization against lowered cost," and tell finance to check whether products "appear to be correlated with each other in terms of growth and cost" [6]. They also name what ties products together: technical coupling, and growth linked by brand, news or cross-promotion [6]. That check is what makes the trade safe, because planning for only some launches to land works like pooling (Section 6.3): independent bets average out. Illustratively, four independent launches each half likely to land will usually deliver about two; all four land only about one time in sixteen (0.5⁴ ≈ 6%). Tie all four to one model release (or one strategy, partner or marketing date), and they land or slip together. Half the time all four land, and a plan for two is short by two. So name any shared driver in the register, and apply a portfolio haircut (planning for fewer successes than were declared) only within groups of bets that lack one. Name the driver; don't infer independence from a low measured correlation. Risk managers warn that dependence goes "beyond simple linear correlation," and the tails are where it shows [A4].

The same idea can size the launch reserve. Holding each launch's high scenario on its own is, in the chapter's terms, a sum of peaks [7]; the same pooling logic applies to launches. Hixson and Guliani already collapse several products' upside into one plan, with someone in a position to resolve conflicts [6]. The chapter pairs centralized inventory with a correlation check [7]. *One way to size it:* hold one reserve for a group of launches with no shared driver, sized to the group's high. Then give each launch a ranked claim on it (Section 8.3). Illustratively, four independent launches each have a 25,000 high slice, each half likely to be needed. Four separate slices make 100,000. At the 80th percentile, the group needs 75,000. Tie the four to one model release and they land together, so the group needs all 100,000. The chapter's own advice applies: first find which parts of a forecast "are correlated and which can be treated as independent" [7]. Figure 27 draws the two cases, and Figure 28 the reserve each one needs.

blocks.heading: 6.7 Supply has step changes too
blocks.markdown:
The new site promised for one date now has another. Supply moves in steps too: a new site comes online, or a hardware generation changes shapes and coefficients (Section 5.3). A vendor rations a constrained part, a decommission retires a block of capacity, or a supply shock delays everything at once. No trend predicts these; someone must declare them. Auxon's authors list a slipped cluster delivery, alongside a service's efficiency regression, among the events that break a hand-built plan [1].

Supply declarations firm up in stages of their own: planned, contracted, under construction, delivered, live. Utilities and operators already report their power this way, with contracted load far ahead of what is under construction or active [68, 92] (Appendix B).

Supply can go live in phases, too. The SRE chapter describes phased delivery that brings basic compute, power and network online months early [7]. It replaces treating capacity as a binary "ready" state, and the early capacity carries a higher risk of stockouts [7]. Public examples exist elsewhere. One AI campus's first phase, "two buildings and 200+ megawatts," was "expected to be energized in the first half of 2025" [93]. Alberta's grid operator allocated an interim connection limit of 1,200 MW and moved other large-load requests to a second phase [94].

Here's where the two sides can meet; the parts are the sources', the field is my exploration. The chapter already sorts work this way, routing work "resilient to transient capacity shortfalls" to the early phases [7]. It calls the property *stockout resiliency*, and has clients tag their own traffic [7]. Hixson and Guliani ask each product what happens if growth exceeds planned capacity [6]. My exploration is to make it a number, with a duration, on every declaration. So it helps to ask each declaration one more question: how much shortfall, for how long, can it take? Call it *shortfall tolerance*. Demand that declares some can be pegged to a site that's only partly live, or hold an over-issued entitlement (Section 6.1). Demand that declares none waits for firm supply. And since a higher availability tier is a driver that raises the rate (Section 5.2), a declared tolerance should lower it. *My guess* is that this field, more than any forecast, decides how much early supply a fleet can use.

So score each supply declaration like a demand declaration, promised size and date against actual (Section 9.2, mechanism 11). A planner who discounts demand intents but takes supply promises at face value has half an outside view. The mirror holds too. A supply team that commits to a demand signal that changes every month inside its lead time has no plan to keep. And its own supplier scores it the same way (Section 6.2).

**Slips travel.** A supply slip opens the approval-allocation gap from the supply side: demand approved against a promised building or generation has nowhere to land. A late transformer delays the building, then every rack and turn-up already committed on the old date; the slipped batches then queue at turn-up together (Section 6.2). Nor does value arrive in proportion. A rack missing one cable isn't 99% of a rack. A training cluster with one block of its network missing may not run the job it was built for at all (Section 11). So fulfillment watches the scarcest small part as closely as the most expensive one. Figure 29 puts supply's stages beside demand's, and follows one slip.

blocks.heading: 6.7 Supply has step changes too
blocks.markdown:
Supply steps are usually lumpier than demand steps: one building's slip reaches every launch it serves. Tie a long-lead supply step to the portfolio, not one launch, and it stays fungible when any launch moves. A supply slip is an envelope change in time, handled as a re-cut (Section 9.1); a shock across many layers is the same re-cut, larger.

**Decommission is negative supply.** Flux records large-scale decommissioning of servers in three regions, "resulting in a reduction of supply in those regions," and manages "projected regional capacity deficits such as those caused by regional hardware refresh" [2]. A retirement is a supply order with a minus sign. It has a date, and it slips, usually because tenants can't migrate off in time. And old racks in an existing building usually have to leave before new ones can use their power and floor. So a slipped decommission can stall a delivery that arrived on time. In my experience, the fastest bridge for a late new site is often an older one. Refreshing it or deferring its decommission gives worse hardware, sooner, where it isn't in the new hardware's way.

**Check supply for shared drivers.** The correlation check of Section 6.6 works for supply too. Four new sites with independent risks will usually deliver most of what was promised; if all four wait on the same transformer supplier or the same utility, they slip together. So the supply register names shared dependencies, and the plan counts on supply averaging out only where it really is independent. *My guess*, and it is only a guess, is that in a tight market lead times stretch together across vendors, because every queue fills at once. If so, supply errors average out least exactly when it matters most, and the cautious lead time of Section 8 should be more cautious then.

blocks.heading: 7. A worked example (all numbers illustrative)
blocks.markdown:
*In short: one service, one caller, invented numbers. The forecast lands within 4%, the bill lands 30% over, and each piece of the miss goes to whoever moved it.*

Sections 5 and 6 took the pieces one at a time. Here they meet in one case, the year-end review of Section 1.

**The setup.** Service X is a shared document store whose calls run server-side queries; Product A is its largest caller. The numbers are invented, and machine counts and dollars are kept small so the arithmetic is easy to follow.

**The common unit** is Section 6.1's invented *normalized machine unit* (NMU), weighted by component cost, 80% for cores and 20% for memory. A standard machine (50 cores, 200 GB) is 1 NMU, so a high-memory machine with 600 GB is 0.8 + 0.2 × 3 = **1.4 NMU**. A core is 0.016 NMU (0.8 ÷ 50 cores) and a GB 0.001 (0.2 ÷ 200 GB).

**The rate card.** X prices only CPU: $0.12 per busy core-hour, the pool's cost over practical capacity, here half of installed cores.

**Why installed is twice busy.** Two buffers with different owners multiply. Surviving the loss of one of three failure domains takes 1.5 times peak, owned by reliability engineering. Holding latency means CPU at most 75% busy, a further 4/3 of queueing headroom, owned by X. If the latency target must hold even with a domain down, the two multiply: 1.5 × 4/3 = 2.0 installed cores for every busy one. The 4/3 is a flat rule, kept simple for the example; queueing headroom shrinks as a share of a larger pool (Section 6.3) [84]. Many teams accept degraded latency during a failure and run hotter, which needs less.

**How A is billed.** On its realized peak, held flat for the year: a simplification of charging its coincident-peak contribution hour by hour. X's release and the power re-pricing below take effect from the start of the year.

**Declare.** A declares next year's peak at 500,000 requests per second, up from 400,000. That's 40,000 of organic growth on A's trend, and 60,000 from a feature launch. The launch is a step change with no history, planned for the start of the second quarter.

The launch reached the forum in stages (Section 5.4; stage timing varies by launch, and Figure 22's is generic):

- **At the annual cycle**, as an intent of 40,000 to 100,000.
- **Dated, two quarters before launch**, with a base of 60,000 and a high of 90,000.
- **Configured, one quarter before launch**, with two regions and the data it would store.

The planner entered the intent at 60,000 (illustrative), where comparable intents had actually landed, and the dated base later confirmed it. So A's declared demand is the organic forecast plus 60,000.

X's coefficient is 0.4 calls per request × 2.5 ms per call = 1.0 ms per request, so busy cores rise from 400 to 500. A's plan is 500 × 8,760 h × $0.12 = **$525,600**, up from $420,480.

**Approve.** 100 busy cores × 2.0 = 200 installed cores. The intake asks only about CPU, so the forum approves four standard machines, **4 NMU**. The high scenario would add 30 busy cores, 60 installed; following Section 6.5, the forum names a bridge for them rather than buying them.

**Fulfill.** Here's the catch: X's memory grows with stored data, not requests. A's data in X will grow by 16 TB, most of it from the launch. That figure is sized at configuration on the dated base volume, and re-sized once actual data is known. At an illustrative 100 GB of memory per TB stored (including failure reserve), 16 TB needs 1.6 TB of memory. Four standard machines supply 0.8 TB.

- **Naively**, the ask needs eight standard machines, **8 NMU**, with half their CPU stranded.
- **Re-shaped**, two standard and two high-memory machines supply exactly 200 cores and 1.6 TB for **4.8 NMU** (1 + 1 + 1.4 + 1.4). That's what the ask would have cost (200 × 0.016 + 1,600 × 0.001) had the intake asked about memory.

The fulfillment ledger (Section 9.2, mechanism 5) records 4.0 approved, 4.8 as the cheapest feasible allocation, and a **0.8 NMU gap**. The gap's named owner can fund it, phase the launch or ask X to shrink its working set. A higher memory weight, as when memory prices run high, would only widen the gap. Figure 30 counts the machines.

blocks.heading: 7. A worked example (all numbers illustrative)
blocks.markdown:
Then the clocks bite. In this example, high-memory machines take two quarters to arrive; standard machines come from X's stocked pool in weeks. In months from launch:

- **Month −6:** the high-memory commit point. The launch was only dated, and the intake asked nothing about stored data.
- **Month −3:** the memory need surfaced at configuration, and the machines were ordered.
- **Month 0:** launch.
- **Month +3:** the machines arrive, a quarter after launch.

In Figure 22's terms, the memory question arrived after the machines' dot: the two-clock failure of Section 6.5.

Until the machines land, the ledger carries a dated bridge. It can be four more standard machines from the stocked pool, run for their memory with their CPU stranded (the naive fulfillment, as a bridge). Or it can be older high-memory machines kept past decommission, at a power and efficiency premium. A pool draw also leaves a replenishment owed, with a date and an owner, or the next team needing a standard machine finds four fewer.

The rate card sees none of this: A's data drives the memory, and X charges only for CPU. Without a second driver, the 0.8 NMU reappears next cycle as an unexplained rise in the CPU rate, paid by every caller for growth one caller caused.

**Actuals.** A's volume lands at 480,000 requests per second, within 4%. Two things A didn't control moved:

- A release of X raised CPU per call to 3.125 ms (α = 1.25 ms per request).
- X's rate rose to $0.13 after a sharp re-pricing of its power contract.

A's cost is 600 busy cores × 8,760 × $0.13 = **$683,280**, 30% over plan. Split by term:

| Term | Calculation | Effect | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Volume | (480k − 500k) × 1.0 ms = −20 cores × 8,760 × $0.12 | −$21,024 | Product A |
| Coefficient | 480k × 0.25 ms = +120 cores × 8,760 × $0.12 | +$126,144 | Service X (its release) |
| Rate | 600 cores × 8,760 × $0.01 | +$52,560 | Service X, with finance |
| **Total** | | **+$157,680** | |

Figure 31 draws the same split as a waterfall.

figure.caption: Figure 31. A forecast within 4% and a bill 30% over plan. Split the variance by term and each piece gets an owner; the two terms A did not own add up to more than the whole overrun.

The terms A did not own total +$178,704, more than the +$157,680 (+30.0%) overrun. Illustrative numbers.

blocks.heading: 7. A worked example (all numbers illustrative)
blocks.markdown:
Read the table as three swaps, one term at a time: plan $525,600; actual volume, $504,576; actual coefficient, $630,720; actual rate, $683,280. The order matters a little (Section 5.2). Put the rate first and its piece is 500 × 8,760 × $0.01 = $43,800, volume −$22,776 and coefficient +$136,656: the same +$157,680, with $8,760 moved off the rate piece.

Supply missed too: 600 busy cores need 1,200 installed against 1,000 planned. The extra 200 installed cores (four standard machines, 4 NMU) came from bridges. Until they landed, X ran inside its own buffers, below its planned redundancy and latency targets: a dated ledger item owned by X.

**Size and timing.** The 20,000 shortfall was all the launch's; organic growth landed on trend. The launch delivered 40,000, two-thirds of its base, six weeks late. As Section 6.6's table predicts for this billing rule, the size miss shows only as A's smaller bill in the volume term, and the slip shows in no term.

This year the slip cost A nothing it could see, and even eased X's shortage. At the drifted coefficient, organic demand alone (440,000 requests per second × 1.25 ms = 550 busy cores, 1,100 installed) needed more than the 1,000 planned. Two errors that offset each other are luck, not a plan working.

Now suppose the coefficient had held, so the launch's 60 busy cores, 120 installed, were really there, waiting. An installed core costs the pool $0.06 an hour (the $0.12 busy-core rate spread over twice as many installed cores). Six weeks is 1,008 hours, so about $7,258 of launch capacity sits idle, split two ways:

| Launch capacity | Installed cores | Idle cost | Who sees it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Used, but six weeks late | 80 (two-thirds) | About $4,838 for the six weeks | No one: A pays it inside its flat bill, as above |
| Never used | 40 (one-third) | About $2,419 for the six weeks, and it runs all year | X's unused line |
| Total, first six weeks | 120 | About $7,258 | |

The never-used third doesn't stop at six weeks. The 40 installed cores built for the 20,000 that never arrived are billed to no one. As 20 busy-core equivalents of practical capacity, they put 20 × 8,760 h × $0.12 = $21,024 on X's unused line. That's A's favorable volume term, seen from X's side. X owns the line, but nothing books it to A's launch, which caused it (Section 6.6).

**The review.** A's leader says, reasonably, that the team hit its number and is billed for someone else's miss. The decomposition makes that conversation short and leaves four questions.

**Should X have versioned the change when it shipped?** Yes. Illustratively, with both of Section 5.2's alerts live, the coefficient miss would have reached X as a ticket long before the bill.

**Does A pay the coefficient term?** On this year's bill, yes: A is billed its busy cores at X's rate, so the $126,144 reaches A unless a rule moves it. The decomposition assigns accountability, not payment. In my judgment, this case needs a rule agreed with finance before any miss. Under it, the forum scores the term against X's efficiency commitment (Section 9.2, mechanism 7). Then it decides whether a central reserve holds A's budget harmless for the year. Without one, the pieces have owners in the meeting but not on the bill.

**Who carries the bridge premiums?** X's release caused the CPU bridges, so X does. Since X recovers its costs through its rate, the forum holds the premium outside the rate (Section 6.4). It sits as an unrecovered variance on X's own line, reported against its efficiency commitment. The memory bridge and this year's 0.8 NMU trace to a gap in the intake design, owned by planning with X. No published driver attributes them to a consumer, so they go to the unallocated line, with both named as owners.

**Who pays for the memory itself?** The hardest one. A's data caused it, so by this paper's principle A should pay. But no published driver told A so, and the forum rules that a new driver applies from its effective date, not retroactively.

Without the decomposition, the meeting is an argument about fault, and A pads next year's declaration. Figure 32 draws the review as decisions.

blocks.heading: 7. A worked example (all numbers illustrative)
blocks.markdown:
**Re-fit.** X adds a second driver, data stored, with its own coefficient (memory per GB stored) and rate, logged with an effective date. Its intake now asks for stored data as a range at intent and a figure once dated. That's because memory is X's slowest dimension to source, and the dated stage falls right at its commit point. It also shows A's 500k ask beside its 480k actual.

**A's launch joins the record** by stage: intent 40,000–100,000, dated base 60,000 and high 90,000, actual 40,000, six weeks late. It landed below the 60,000 where comparable intents had, and will move the next estimate.

**The three prices now give three answers:**

- The **average rates** for CPU and memory set A's budget.
- The **long-run incremental cost** of A's growth is memory-driven: 4.8 NMU rather than 4.0, a 20% premium that belongs on the memory driver.
- The **shadow price** falls on whichever dimension binds. Under the naive eight-machine fulfillment, that's memory, which is why re-shaping saves 3.2 NMU. Once the coefficient drifted, 600 busy cores needed 1,200 installed against 1,000 planned, so CPU ran out first, and that's what the bridges were buying.

Every piece now sits on an artifact with an owner and a date. What the example doesn't show is how to catch the memory question in time. Section 8 does.

blocks.heading: 8. The commit-point method
blocks.markdown:
*In short: one launch, every supply layer, eight steps on one page. For each layer, ask when it must be ordered in a slow case, and how firm the launch will be by then. Then ask what to commit, in what form, with whom owning the rest.*

Section 7 shows what goes wrong, not the walk that would have prevented it. A planner who agrees with Sections 5 and 6 still faces a blank page on Monday: which layer first, which number where, who signs what? This section offers that walk. It puts the earlier pieces in order: stages (Section 5.4), supply layers and contracts (Section 6.2), and bridges and pegging (Section 6.4). Then come commit points and change bands (Section 6.5), and the ways a step can miss on either side (Sections 6.6 and 6.7). It's a way to think a launch through, not a model; Appendix A has the one-page worksheet and the full walk-through.

blocks.heading: 8.1 The idea in one paragraph
blocks.markdown: Every supply layer must be ordered by some date, and by then the launch has only firmed up so far. So for each layer ask: when must this be ordered, if the order is slow? How firm will the launch be by then? Given that, what do we commit, in what form, and who owns the rest? Then net against what you have, agree how much the launch may still change at each stage, and write it down where supply can answer it. Figure 33 shows the walk and what it writes down.

figure.label: Figure 33
figure.caption: Figure 33. The walk ends in artifacts, not a number. Each step writes into a register, a map, a ledger or supply's answer, so the decision can be checked and defended later.
figure.alt: Eight steps in two groups. Read (worksheet Part A): list the layers and their lead times in the slow case; find each layer's need date and commit point; read the stage and the range still open at each commit point, and whether the driving attribute is known. Decide (worksheet Part B and footer): choose how far up the range to cover; net against what you have; split each layer into firm, flexible and named; agree change bands per stage; write it down and get supply's answer. The steps flow into four artifacts: the declaration register entry with its bands (mechanism 12), a commit-point map line per layer (13), the supply request and supply's answer (11), and the fulfillment ledger line (5), whose net and committed columns come from steps 5 and 6. A decision note is added where a commit point fell before the event that resolves it. Method steps are numbered pills, unlike the funnel's numbered squares.

blocks.heading: 8.2 The eight steps
blocks.markdown:
1. **List the layers and their lead times, using the slow case.** Take every layer the declaration touches: power and space, network, each machine shape, parts, turn-up, placement. Write each one's usual lead time and a cautious one, near the slow end of what you've seen (Section 6.2). A public value (Appendix B) is a sanity check, not your number. *Why:* in my experience (Section 6.2), deliveries are rarely early and sometimes very late.
2. **Find each layer's need date and commit point.** Work back from launch. The ready-for-service date sits ahead of launch by the testing the launch needs. Each layer's need date is the start of the layer after it; its commit point is that need date minus the cautious lead time. *Why:* layers stack, so a slow layer's real deadline is earlier than launch day suggests.
3. **Read the stage at each commit point, and the range still open.** Lay the declaration's stages (Section 5.4) on the same timeline. At each commit point, note the stage reached and the range still open, from the stage's record, not only the team's word. Then ask: is the attribute that drives this layer known by then? Memory drives a high-memory order; region drives power and network. If not, pick one of Section 6.5's three choices and write it down. Where the commit point comes before any declaration exists, as power and shell often do, the portfolio envelope serves that layer; record the launch's claim on it. *Why:* this question would have caught Section 7's memory problem in time.
4. **Choose how far up the range to cover.** Use the shortage-to-idle ratio agreed for this layer and kind of demand (Section 10.2), with supply's idle cost and liability terms. That ratio is the cost of running short against the cost of holding spare (Section 6.3). Failing that, start from Section 6.5's illustrative table (for turn-up, the ratio sets how much rate to staff). Convert the point into the layer's units: positions, machines of each shape, turn-up slots. *Why:* shortage and spare cost differently on each layer, so one level for all is wrong somewhere.
5. **Net against what you already have.** The net need is the target, minus what's on hand, on order or due back from reclaim, plus capacity due to retire that current load depends on. Each of those is a forecast too, so give each a date and an owner. A deferred retirement can bridge only if its hardware isn't in the space or power the new hardware needs, and a draw on a stocked pool leaves a replenishment owed. *Why:* each number subtracted is a forecast too, and a reclaim that doesn't happen looks like a supply failure (Section 6).
6. **Split each layer into firm, flexible and named.** *Firm* covers up to the base, as a plain order. *Flexible* covers from the base up to the step 4 target, as options, cancelable or reschedulable orders, or a named launch reserve. *Named* covers the rest, as a bridge with an owner and a ready-by date and, at the very top, admission control. Figure 34 draws the split. Since the most common timing miss is a slip (Section 6.6), prefer the right to push a delivery out over the right to cancel it. *Why:* each slice gets the cheapest form that covers it, and none is left without an owner.
7. **Agree change bands per stage.** With the declaring team, agree how far size and date may move at each stage before the move becomes a priced event (Section 6.5). Supply signs the same bands, because they're its buying assumptions. Bands tighter than the stage's record supports make every launch an exception. *Why:* a band says when the declaration has left the range supply bought against.
8. **Write it down, and get supply's answer.** Record the result in four artifacts. The first two are the declaration register entry, with its bands (mechanism 12), and one commit-point map line per layer (mechanism 13). The others are the supply request and supply's answer (mechanism 11), and the fulfillment ledger line, with net and committed columns (mechanism 5). Where a commit point fell before the event that resolves it, add a decision note: what was known, when, by whom, and what would have changed it. *Why:* an approval is firm only once supply has answered it, and a written decision can be defended later.

From 60,000 to the 70,000 target is flexible: options, reschedulable orders or a named reserve. Above 70,000 to 90,000 is named: a bridge with an owner and a ready-by date, then admission control. blocks.heading: 8.3 What each side owes the other
heading_path: 8.3 What each side owes the other
blocks.markdown:
This is where "approval is not allocation," the second claim of Section 1, becomes an exchange with two halves.

**Planning owes supply** six things, per layer and before its commit point. The first three are the net requirement by shape, site and need date; the stage and open range, not just a point; and the signed change band. Next are the substitutes the team will accept (other shapes, other sites, a smaller first phase, a later date). Last come the ramp, not just the peak, and the launch's rank under shortage.

**Supply answers each line** with a *dated commit* (quantity, date, confidence, any substituted shape) or a *named gap* (how much, by when, why, and a proposed bridge with its owner). Until then, the approval is uncommitted (Section 6.1). Pegging each order to its declaration (Section 6.4) lets a late delivery be traced to the launches it hits, and a slipped launch hand its supply to someone else.

Both sides get scored: supply on promised against actual, demand on how much it changed inside supply's lead time. Figure 35 follows one ask across the four parties.

blocks.heading: 8.4 The same launch, walked through
blocks.markdown:
Appendix A walks Section 7's launch through all eight steps, with one added assumption that makes memory scale with the launch's size. A cautious lead time and a real need date move the high-memory commit point to −11, while the launch is still an intent. That's where step 3 catches the missing stored-data question. Who pays for the landing still follows the rule agreed with finance. The table compares the two:

| | Section 7 as written | With the method (illustrative) |
|---|---|---|
| High-memory commit point | −6, at dated | −11, at intent |
| Stored data asked | At −3 (configured) | At −12 (intent), as a range |
| High-memory machines arrive | +3, a quarter after launch | By −2 |
| Bridge during launch | Four standard machines run for memory, or old machines past decommission | None needed at the base; named in advance above 70,000 |
| Size miss | Lands on X's unused line, booked to no declaration | Same cost, recorded against A's declaration as a band breach |
| Slip | Invisible | Recorded; the launch reserve re-pegged to another tenant |
| Cost of the approach | — | About 1.0 NMU held above the base, and a nine-month view of a range still open |

The method doesn't make the launch more accurate. It moves the hard question to the date it was needed, and it gives every surprise an owner. Its cost shows, too. At 40,000, A's growth needs 160 installed cores against 250 held (five machines, sized to the configured 80th percentile of 70,000). So 90 sit idle, about $47,304 a year. Section 7's plan would have left 40 idle ($21,024), so the method's extra machine accounts for about $26,280. That's the plan working inside its 4:1 ratio for persistent demand, and the band records which declaration the spare waited on. Figure 36 draws the two timelines.

figure.caption: Figure 36. Section 7's launch with and without the method. A cautious lead time and a real need date move the high-memory commit point from −6 to −11, early enough to ask about stored data. The spare it buys has a price, and an owner. Illustrative.

With the method: power commits at −20, stored data is asked at −12, high-memory commits at −11, machines are on the dock by −2, ready for service at −1; no bridge at the base. The cost is about 1.0 NMU of spare, about $26,280 a year more idle at the 40,000 landing. Illustrative.

blocks.heading: 8.5 Where it comes from, and what it adds
heading_path: 8.5 Where it comes from, and what it adds
blocks.markdown:
Almost nothing in the method is new on its own. Hixson and Guliani supply the frame: "You should plan at least as far ahead as the order time for your resources," use fungibility to delay deciding which product gets the capacity, and keep step changes itemized so the process can learn [6]. Their lead-time table, which ends at "Ready to serve," is step 2 in outline [6]. Olavson's team supplies the base-and-high consensus and execution to the high scenario [8]. Manufacturing supplies netting and time fences (standard practice) and postponement [73]. The operations literature supplies quantity flexibility [70, 71] and chained flexibility [77]. Textbooks supply the newsvendor formula behind the shortage-to-idle ratio [78], and Dixit and Pindyck the option value of waiting [76].

What the method adds, as far as the sources I could read show, is the walk. That's a fixed order of questions applied to one declaration across every layer, ending in signed artifacts. Its new parts would be commit points read against the stage, on a cautious lead time and a real need date, and a standing question about the driving attribute. The rest would be a firm, flexible and named split per layer, bands tied to the stages, and a supply answer per line. The 2026 SRE chapter supplies pieces of the read half (Section 3) [7]. Its Meet case study ran a daily loop asking whether there were enough resources for the load expected a week out [7]. As far as the public record I could read shows, the per-layer walk tied to a launch's stage isn't there.

blocks.heading: 8.6 What it doesn't claim, and where it might go
heading_path: 8.6 What it doesn't claim, and where it might go
blocks.markdown:
It's **not a model**: the ten-outcome lists, ratios and bands write judgment down; they estimate nothing. It's **untested**: if it works, Section 9.2's tests should show fewer orders placed after their commit point, smaller bridge premiums, and band breaches growing rarer as records build up. It has **blind spots**: coefficient drift (mechanism 3 catches it), correlated launches (Section 6.6's shared-driver check does) and demand nobody can declare (Section 13). And it's **not optimal**. Buying to the 80th percentile on one layer and the median on the next is a rule of thumb. It's for layers that work together (Section 6.5, condition 1), not a joint optimum. A data scientist could do better.

Three explorations, labeled as such:

- **A fast lane.** Hixson and Guliani describe one: fungible pooled resources, provisioned "much more quickly than their full lead time" [6]. *One way to think about it:* Section 7's stocked pool is a fast lane, dearer than the slow lane but able to wait until the launch is configured. Its size is a decision. For example, if configured asks usually move by a tenth of their dated figure, and next quarter's dated asks total 50 machines, start from a pool of about 5 machines. Add cover for its own replenishment time. *My guess* is that with two lanes, the slow lane can be bought lower than Section 6.5's table suggests.
- **Re-pegging.** In the walk-through, the six-week slip freed a launch reserve for six weeks. *Speculation:* across enough launches, re-pegging may absorb a large share of timing misses at almost no cost. Nobody has measured it in public, as far as the sources show.
- **A simulation.** A spreadsheet can stress-test the hand calculation. Draw a few hundred random years from each declaration's stage ranges and each layer's lead-time spread. Then count which launches end up short, and because of which layer. It could show whether per-layer ratios come close to the best joint answer, and what bands and shared drivers change. That's a stress test, not a validation, and its answers would depend on the data used.

blocks.heading: 9. The operating discipline: keeping the agreement
heading_path: 9. The operating discipline: keeping the agreement
blocks.markdown:
*In short: thirteen mechanisms, each an artifact with an owner, keep the agreement true from one cycle to the next.*

Sections 7 and 8 built the artifacts for one launch. The harder problem is keeping them true, cycle after cycle, as people, budgets and coefficients move. Much of this is published. There's a monthly consensus forecast approved by customers, finance and operations, with accountability metrics [8], and capacity contracts with a plan of record approved by leadership [31]. There's also an intake that already knows each team's allocation, usage and idle capacity [34]. And there's the SRE chapter's plan of record (Section 3) [7]. What I haven't found, in the sources I could read, is one set of artifacts and owners that joins them with coefficient ownership, a fulfillment ledger and a declaration register. That joining, argued from practice, is what this paper offers.

blocks.heading: 9.1 A cadence that turns uncertainty into commitment
heading_path: 9. The operating discipline: keeping the agreement
9.1 A cadence that turns uncertainty into commitment
blocks.markdown:
At the annual review, one slide sums every team's ask; the next shows finance's number. The cadence exists to close that gap. Each cycle commits only what its lead time forces. The cycles nest, slowest outside:

1. **Annual:** set the envelope and first cut line; pre-position the longest-lead resources; sign forecasts and efficiency commitments.
2. **Quarterly:** specify demand in driver units and shapes, and re-forecast against actuals. Hold a supply review (what supply can commit, where it can't, which risks moved), and place medium-lead orders on its answers.
3. **Monthly:** supply updates commits and named gaps; re-rank launches against supply; move the cut line.
4. **Continuous steering:** arbitrate, broker, run bridges, keep the fulfillment ledger.
5. **Post-launch:** actuals become the next coefficient; log discontinuities; decompose variance.

Each level serves one band of Figure 22's commit points, from intents (annual) to live launches (steering). It's sales and operations planning for internal infrastructure [23], nested by lead time as in hierarchical production planning [3]. Operators publish versions: a monthly rolling four-quarter consensus [8], quarterly plans built on the expected outcome of earlier quarters [1], and budgets whose quarterly or annual boundaries add to lead time [6]. In my experience, the step most often missing is the supply review. That's a fixed point between the demand review and the executive decision, where supply brings its own plan, constraints and risks. Figure 37 lays the cycles on a calendar, with the supply review highlighted.

9.1 A cadence that turns uncertainty into commitment
blocks.markdown:
**Closing the gap with finance.** In my experience, finance sets the envelope top-down, from cash, committed depreciation and, at a public company, capital guidance given to investors. Declared demand sums higher. As Hixson and Guliani put it, "it will almost certainly be impossible to fund the capacity requested of each product at its most optimistic growth rate without any improvements in efficiency" [6]. So the envelope draws a cut line through the ranked list, and everything below it is named, not silently trimmed pro rata.

Envelopes move after signing, too. A mid-cycle cut or pull-in is a re-sign event: the cut line moves, and displaced claims are named in an order agreed beforehand (the *re-cut order*). A plan that absorbs a 10% cut (illustrative) by moving one line survives; one renegotiated team by team does not. Figure 38 follows a cut, a slip or a shortage through the re-cut.

**Fitting calendars you don't control.** Close the annual horizon a few weeks before finance's budget lock, and write commitments into teams' own goals. In my experience, a forum that meets only when decisions are due gets executives; one that meets more often gets delegates.

**No surprises in the room.** In my experience, a decision meeting goes well when nobody in it sees their number for the first time. So walk the numbers up in steps. First, take the baselines to the leaders who own the biggest launches, for their read on what matters. Then gather demand from the teams, and take it back to those leaders to rank and trim. Only then put the top-down view and the bottom-up one side by side for the executives. Finance, and whoever approves orders, come after that, and they'll want the business cases for the largest asks already written. In the room, have answers ready. When a question has no answer yet, say so, take it back to the engineers, and bring the answer back by a date. That's how a forum learns to trust the next answer.

**Saying no.** Planning must be able to refuse. Some refusals only reflect calendars out of step, and aligning the calendars removes them. For real scarcity, the refusal is a mechanism: written, at intake, citing the binding dimension and the cut line, and owned by the forum. It comes with a path forward: a re-shaped ask, a phased launch, placement elsewhere or a dated slot next cycle. A refusal with no path forward gets routed around, and capacity routed around is no longer planned.

Where does the right to refuse come from? In my experience, rarely from rank; planners usually have none. It comes from the number and the team's own signature. A team that signed a forecast or utilization commitment, and is far outside it, can be asked to wait, and that's defensible because the team wrote the terms. Keep the hold for serious misses, and say in advance what counts as one. A gate used for small misses feels like punishment, and gets routed around too. In the first year, enforcement rests on the planner's persuasion, which doesn't scale and doesn't win friends. Mechanism 7 is the way out: write the commitments into the annual agreement, so after that the agreement enforces them, not a person. Once the planning calendar matches the launch calendar, teams know the dates and what they signed, and they unblock themselves by keeping their word.

blocks.heading: 9.2 Thirteen mechanisms
heading_path: 9. The operating discipline: keeping the agreement
blocks.markdown:
**You'll know it's working when…** Seven of the mechanisms have a test that can fail:

- **2, prior ask beside prior actual:** forecast bias falls within a number of cycles stated in advance. If it doesn't, the column is decoration.
- **3, coefficient register and versioned rate card:** variance from unannounced changes shrinks.
- **5, fulfillment ledger:** fewer launches are delayed for capacity. If not, the gap lies in lead time or turn-up.
- **8, efficiency landing rule:** re-funded recovery lasts, and clawed-back recovery decays.
- **11, supply plan of record and commitment register:** the gap between promised and actual delivery dates narrows. And with a supply answer for every ask, fewer approvals turn out to be undesigned gaps; the paired indicators show whether late supply followed late asks.
- **12, declaration register:** scoring declarations by stage makes intents' size error stable enough to discount, if not smaller.
- **13, commit-point map:** fewer orders are placed after their commit point, and their bridge premiums shrink.

The other six (1, 4, 6, 7, 9 and 10) have no test of this kind yet. For them, watch the Indicator column.

Nine decision rights sit outside the Owner column:

- **Overriding the cut line:** a named executive, logged with the displaced claim.
- **Re-cutting the plan when the envelope changes:** the forum, in ranked order, with finance.
- **Promoting, demoting or expiring a declaration:** planning, on the stage's evidence or a missed target date (Section 9.3).
- **Re-signing after a reorganization:** the new accountable leader.
- **Interim owners for orphaned coefficients:** planning.
- **The shortage-to-idle ratios:** finance and product jointly; supply provides the cost of idle and the liability terms.
- **Change bands inside each lead time:** supply and planning, signed by the declaring team, with finance agreeing who pays for a change outside them.
- **Answering an ask with a commit or a gap, and accepting a substitute shape or site:** supply.
- **Reliability buffers:** reliability engineering.

Figure 40 sets the nine rights against the roles.

blocks.heading: 9.3 Notes on the mechanisms
heading_path: 9. The operating discipline: keeping the agreement
blocks.markdown:
**Pre-fill, then confirm.** A blank template returns last year's numbers plus a growth factor. So planning pre-fills the intake from telemetry and current coefficients, and the team adds two things: its driver forecast, and any override of the pre-filled shape, with a reason, signed. Effort goes where the team knows something the planner doesn't.

**Talk before you send the form.** A pre-filled intake still arrives as a form from a stranger. It comes back more credible when the people filling it in have already talked with the person collecting it, one to one, about their own service. So do that before the intake opens. Then gather teams in small groups, and let each one say what it believes its own biggest launches are. Hand out the pre-filled intake at the end of that session. *My guess* is that teams pad less in front of the peers they'll compete with for the same envelope. Either way, the planner leaves knowing who holds what and what's coming, which is most of what brokering needs later (Section 6.4).

**Prior actuals in the intake.** When the intake shows "you asked for X and used Y," the padding talk happens before the ask. Bias (a governance problem) is tracked apart from dispersion (a buffer input), and step changes are scored by stage (Section 5.4).

**Declarations expire.** A placeholder can hold capacity for a year for a launch nobody mentions anymore. So set a clock: an intent that hasn't advanced by its target date leaves the envelope unless re-confirmed, and a configured launch's grant lapses if its date passes unconfirmed. The slip becomes a recorded event. Grid operators learned this the expensive way. Speculative requests helped back up U.S. interconnection queues, and FERC's 2023 reform moved to "first-ready, first-served," with readiness deposits and withdrawal penalties [A6]. One public analogue is automated: the SRE chapter describes AI sweeps that reclaim "inactive or expired ML quota credits" [7].

A sweep is only as fair as the rules it follows. The chapter notes that easy access to capacity reduces hoarding [7]; a harsh reclaim, I'd argue, brings it back. So an automated sweep should follow the landing rule (mechanism 8) and honor any right of recall (Section 10.4). It should also log each reclaim like an override, since the chapter warns that "agents can behave in surprising ways" [7]. *My guess* is that teams will judge a sweep less by how much it frees than by whether what they return comes back when needed.

**Ask for slow attributes first** (Section 6.5). And ask which substitutes the team would accept (other shapes, regions, a smaller first phase, a later date); each one is free supply flexibility.

**Shortage rules come before the shortage.** The re-cut order handles a smaller envelope. A delivery short in one shape at one site needs its own rule: who goes short first. Agree it in the forum beforehand; supply carries it out. Written during the shortage, it's a negotiation. And don't split a shortage pro rata. Supply-chain theory shows that allocation rules rewarding bigger orders make buyers "order more than they need to gain a more favorable allocation" [A5]. As I read that result, a ranked list removes the reward: a padded ask only buys capacity its team pays for.

**Efficiency is a funding source.** Under chargeback with no reinvestment rule, a team that cuts its footprint gets a smaller bill at best. At worst, it gets a higher rate once a usage-based denominator shrinks (Section 4). Recovered capacity has to land where the recoverer sees it, as gain-sharing plans recognize [4], while in a lean year finance will rationally want to book it as savings. So agree the split before any recovery is known: for example, shares booked as savings, returned to the recoverer and held centrally. A rule agreed in advance is a contract; one proposed after the savings appear is a request.

The landing rule matters most when the envelope freezes, because then the only capital is what can be freed. For example, if budgets freeze partway into a move from an old platform to a new one, the move has to be paid for out of the old platform. One path is to squeeze both ends at once. On the new side, negotiate requirements down to what the team can genuinely run on: every line removed is capacity nobody has to find. On the old side, work with the service owners to raise utilization, land real optimizations and size new launches tightly: every unit freed pays for the next step. Neither end alone frees enough. The first step is the hardest, because it's paid for before anyone knows what the new platform really needs. So move in small slices. Each one buys headroom and a better read of the exchange rate between old and new (as in Section 5.4, the rollout is the measurement).

**The unallocated line is a trust device.** Most bills have a remainder nobody can attribute. TBM parks unallocated "fallout" in staging buckets with temporary pro-rata splits [38]. The FinOps Foundation describes an "informed ignore," budgeting shared items centrally [21]. Neither names an owner accountable for shrinking it. Finance, not planning, should keep the score, or the indicators become self-assessment.

blocks.heading: 9.4 How to tell if this works
heading_path: 9. The operating discipline: keeping the agreement
9.4 How to tell if this works
blocks.markdown:
Little of this has been measured in public, as far as I can find. The nearest results come from two sources. Olavson's comparison of forecast methods puts component safety stock (the parts buffer of Section 6.3) at about 0.6 times its customer-driven level under triangulation [8]. Triangulation here means customer forecasts checked against statistical ones. Gupta reports that a driver-based intake cut a three-to-four-month planning exercise to about one month [34].

Each mechanism's own test sits with it, in Section 9.2, under *You'll know it's working when…*

blocks.heading: 10. People: the room around the math
heading_path: 10. People: the room around the math
blocks.markdown:
*In short: capacity is a handshake among capital, supply and demand, and the planner brokers it. Then come the seams, overrides, reorganizations and gaming.*

Every capacity plan is a handshake among three parties. **Capital** is finance and the leaders who set the envelope: it has the money, and wants it to buy something. **Demand** is the teams that launch and grow products, and the shared services they call: they have plans, and want capacity on time. **Supply** is whoever turns money into running machines: the supply chain, the sites, the fleet. It has lead times and contracts, and wants a signal it can buy against.

None of the three can close the deal alone. Capital can approve, but it can't deliver. Demand can declare, but it can't fund. Supply can build, but only against a signal that's often late, padded or both. That's where the planner sits: in the middle, usually owning no capacity and no budget.

So what does a planner trade in? In my experience, four things:

- **Information:** what's coming, who holds what, and what supply can really do by when.
- **Timing:** when each question must be asked, so the answer arrives before the order has to be placed.
- **Trust:** numbers that hold up, from a planner who doesn't pad its own.
- **Credible commitments:** signatures that turn one party's promise into something the others can buy against.

The planner owes each corner something different. Capital gets numbers that hold, a cut line that names what falls below it, and early warning of finance decisions dressed as capacity ones. Supply gets signed demand before each commit point, with its stage and range, not churn. Demand gets the same picture as everyone else, a "no" that comes with a path, and capacity back when it gives some up.

The paper's two claims sit on the triangle's edges. A coefficient is the price demand pays capital for what supply provides, so it holds only while all three agree on it. And approval is capital's handshake with demand; allocation is supply's. The gap between them is the third seam (Section 10.1).

A shared service sits on two corners at once: it's supply to its callers and demand to the fleet. That's why the first seam below exists. Section 10.1's Figure 41 draws the triangle, with the seams on its edges.

blocks.heading: 10.1 Three seams
heading_path: 10. People: the room around the math
blocks.markdown:
A platform lead gets blamed for a shortage in one meeting and for the bill in the next. It isn't personal. In my experience, the most persistent conflict in this field is structural, and it runs along three seams.

**The first seam runs between product and platform.** Product is rewarded for launches and growth; platform is measured on cost and reliability, and blamed for both. Section 5.2's identity sits on this seam: volume belongs to product, coefficient and rate to platform. Neither can manage cost alone; the mechanisms keep the conflict productive, not personal.

**The second runs between planning and finance.** Planning thinks in machines, megawatts and lead times; finance, in capital and operating spend, depreciation schedules, and a forecast already given to its own leadership. Some decisions that look purely technical cross this seam:

- A third-party bridge turns capital into operating spend.
- Deferring a decommission extends depreciation on an asset finance had written off its plan.
- An early order commits cash in one fiscal year for capacity charged back over several. So a plan reconciled only to the rate can approve spend the cash budget can't carry.

Each is a finance decision disguised as a capacity decision. Bring finance in only to set the rate, and you'll discover them at the quarterly close.

Finance often distrusts planning's numbers, and it often has reasons. Think of inflated asks, double counting, missing baselines and "just in case" capacity. Add savings promised and never seen, and teams that can't explain their own use of shared services. Trust comes back the slow way. Use one template and one format for every team, so asks can be compared. Put each team's baseline and last year's actual beside its ask (mechanism 2). Ask for a short business case tying the ask to growth, a launch, efficiency or risk. And show constrained supply against ranked demand on one page, with a way to drill down. None of it is clever. It's what makes an ask believable to someone who's been burned before.

**The third seam runs between planning and supply**, and it's where "approval is not allocation" actually lives. Planning approves in a common unit; supply buys parts, racks and buildings on dated contracts with penalties. Demand that changes inside supply's lead time makes every supplier look late; supply that commits without naming its risks makes every approval look firm. So the seam needs five artifacts both sides sign. Four are an answer to every approved ask (Section 8.3), pegging (Section 6.4), change bands and who pays beyond them (Section 6.5), and shortage rules agreed in advance (Section 9.3). The fifth is a definition of done for each handoff: what "delivered," "live" and "ready for service" mean and who accepts each, anchored on Hixson and Guliani's "Ready to serve" [6]. The SRE chapter warns against treating "ready" as binary, so a definition can have phases [7]. Supply gets matching decision rights (Section 9.2). An approval becomes firm when supply has answered it, not when the forum has voted. Figure 41 puts the three seams on the triangle's edges, with what has to cross each.
